Solving large populations on a GPU

Source: vignettes/articles/rxode2-gpu.Rmd
rxode2-gpu.Rmd

Population simulation and estimation solve the same small ODE system for many subjects. The gpu* methods integrate every subject that is waiting to be integrated at the same time: one OpenCL kernel launch with one work-item per subject, after the per-trajectory design of Julia’s DiffEqGPU (Utkarsh et al. 2024). Doses, steady state, lag times, covariates and resets stay on the host and run rxode2’s usual per-subject event code, so any event table that works with a host method works here.

Methods

GPU method Host counterpart Integrator Julia DiffEqGPU
"gpuT54" "t54" Tsitouras 5(4) GPUTsit5()
"gpuVern76" "vern76" Verner 7(6) GPUVern7()
"gpuRos54p" "ros54p" Rodas5P with the analytic Jacobian GPURodas5P()
"gpuT54+gpuRos54p" "t54+ros54p" AutoSwitch on the device –
"gpuVern76+gpuRos54p" "vern76+ros54p" AutoSwitch on the device –

The host counterpart solves any model with the same integrator, so a model can move between the two without changing its numerical method.

Requirements

  • The suggested OpenCL package (with an OpenCL driver for your GPU, or pocl for CPUs) for gpuBackend = "opencl". rxode2 itself links no OpenCL; without the package the methods still run with the CPU build.
  • A device with double precision (cl_khr_fp64), or gpuPrecision = "float".
  • A model whose d/dt() can be written as device code: rxModelVars(model)$flags["gpuSafe"] is 1. Random numbers, linCmt(), matExp(), user R functions and similar keep a model on the host.
library(rxode2)
rxGpuInfo()
#> $available
#> [1] TRUE
#>
#> $fp64
#> [1] TRUE
#>
#> $devices
#>   index                    platform                         device type  fp64
#> 1     1                     rusticl            AMD Radeon Graphics  gpu FALSE
#> 2     2 Portable Computing Language cpu-haswell-AMD Ryzen 7 PRO ...  cpu  TRUE

Simulating 

mod <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1.2)
    tcl <- log(3)
    tv <- log(30)
    eta.ka ~ 0.2
    eta.cl ~ 0.1
    eta.v ~ 0.1
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl) * (wt / 70)^0.75
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(center) <- ka * depot - cl / v * center
    cp <- center / v
  })
}

ev <- et(amt = 300, ii = 12, addl = 6) |>
  et(seq(0, 96, by = 2)) |>
  et(id = 1:20000)
ev$wt <- 70

sim <- rxSolve(mod, ev, method = "gpuRos54p")

The options, all in rxControl():

  • gpuBackend: "auto" (default) uses OpenCL when a device with the requested precision exists and otherwise the CPU build, on cores threads; "opencl" and "cpu" choose explicitly. options(rxode2.gpuBackend = "cpu") sets what "auto" picks.
  • gpuDevice: the device index from rxGpuInfo().
  • gpuPrecision: "double" (default) or "float"; with "float" loosen atol and rtol (for example to 1e-5 and 1e-4).
  • gpuBatch: the most subjects in flight at once (default 16384).

Each subject keeps its own tolerances, so a per-subject tolFactor (or atolRtolFactor_() from nlmixr2est) loosens only that subject.

When a model cannot run on the device

Under gpuBackend = "auto" these solve on the host with a message: a model that is not GPU-safe uses the host counterpart; delay() read outside d/dt(), steady state in a delay() model, resampled covariates, or a registered rxRegisterDydtForce() hook use the model’s default method. An explicit gpuBackend = "opencl" or "cpu" stops rxSolve() with an error instead. Inside an nlmixr2 fit such a solve always uses the host counterpart, whatever gpuBackend says.

Estimation with nlmixr2

nlmixr2 passes rxControl() to every solve, so a fit uses a GPU method by naming it there. This model (from bench/gpu-nlmixr2.R) has a saturable term in its elimination:

library(nlmixr2)
pk <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- log(1.2)
    tcl <- log(3)
    tv <- log(30)
    temax <- log(0.5)
    eta.ka ~ 0.2
    eta.cl ~ 0.1
    eta.v ~ 0.1
    prop.sd <- 0.1
    add.sd <- 0.05
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl)
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    emax <- exp(temax)
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(center) <- ka * depot - cl / v * (1 + emax * center / (center + 50)) * center
    cp <- center / v
    cp ~ add(add.sd) + prop(prop.sd)
  })
}

set.seed(42)
ev <- et(amt = 300, ii = 12, addl = 2, cmt = "depot") |>
  et(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 30, 36)) |>
  et(id = 1:500)
sim <- rxSolve(pk, ev, addDosing = TRUE, returnType = "data.frame")
dat <- sim[, c("id", "time", "evid", "amt", "cmt", "sim")]
names(dat)[names(dat) == "sim"] <- "dv"
dat$dv[dat$evid != 0] <- 0

fit <- nlmixr2(
  pk, dat, "saem",
  control = saemControl(rxControl = rxControl(method = "gpuRos54p"))
)
fitHost <- nlmixr2(
  pk, dat, "saem",
  control = saemControl(rxControl = rxControl(method = "ros54p"))
)

With 500 subjects (bench/gpu-nlmixr2.R, the node described under Timings, 8 threads, seconds):

method backend SAEM FOCEi
liblsoda host 183 10.5
t54 host 179 2.8
ros54p host 284 9.7
"t54+ros54p" host 185 2.9
gpuT54 CPU build 144 4.6
gpuRos54p CPU build 158 4.4
"gpuT54+gpuRos54p" CPU build 140 4.5
gpuT54 OpenCL 112 4.1
gpuRos54p OpenCL 120 7.8
"gpuT54+gpuRos54p" OpenCL 111 12.7
  • SAEM solves every subject’s three chains together, so the GPU methods integrate about 1500 subjects per round. On the L40 the SAEM fit takes 112 s against 179 s for the fastest host method; gpuRos54p takes 120 s against 284 s for ros54p.
  • The device’s share of that is 58 s for 125,451 rounds (0.46 ms each); the host event handling between rounds takes 20 s and nlmixr2’s own SAEM work the rest.
  • With options(rxode2.optExprExpensive = TRUE) the device time drops to 49 s and the gpuT54 fit takes 103 s; the CPU build is slower with it (169 s), so it is off by default.
  • With the driver’s work groups (options(rxode2.gpuLocalSize = 0)) the rounds take 157 s and the fit 210 s.
  • FOCEi solves one subject at a time while it optimizes the etas, so a GPU method runs its host counterpart there.

Timings

All timings are from one node: an NVIDIA L40 (OpenCL, double precision) and an Intel Xeon Gold 6526Y with 8 threads for the host methods, the CPU build and Julia’s EnsembleThreads. Julia’s GPU column is DiffEqGPU’s EnsembleGPUKernel on CUDA. Ensembles: Lorenz on t in [0, 1] and Robertson on [0, 1000], one parameter set per subject, atol = rtol = 1e-8. Times in ms.

Kernels

One round integrating every subject over one interval (bench/gpu-runtime-julia.R, medians of 5):

problem rxode2 / Julia method subjects rxode2 OpenCL Julia CUDA rxode2 CPU build Julia threads
lorenz gpuT54 / GPUTsit5 1e3 3 1.2 2 3.6
lorenz gpuRos54p / GPURodas5P 1e3 8 4.2 5 40
lorenz gpuT54 / GPUTsit5 1e5 18 46 207 393
lorenz gpuVern76 / GPUVern7 1e5 14 40 124 266
lorenz gpuRos54p / GPURodas5P 1e5 30 69 527 3810
robertson gpuRos54p / GPURodas5P 1e5 21 56 322 2424
  • At 1e5 subjects the rxode2 kernels are 2.3 to 2.9 times faster than DiffEqGPU’s CUDA kernels and 9 to 18 times faster than the CPU build.
  • At 1e3 subjects a launch costs more than the integration, and the CPU build is as fast as the device.
  • The end states agree with Julia’s CUDA ones to 7e-10 and its threaded ones to 3e-9.

Whole solves

Whole rxSolve() calls, with setup, event handling and the output data frame included (bench/gpu-solve-julia.R, medians of 3):

problem GPU / host method subjects rxode2 OpenCL Julia CUDA rxode2 host Julia threads
lorenz gpuT54 / t54 1e4 38 5 145 29
lorenz gpuRos54p / ros54p 1e4 47 7 645 341
robertson gpuRos54p / ros54p 1e4 42 5 170 213
lorenz gpuT54 / t54 1e5 197 41 2736 405
lorenz gpuRos54p / ros54p 1e5 235 73 5546 3799
robertson gpuRos54p / ros54p 1e5 207 53 3336 2399
  • The GPU methods are 14 to 24 times faster than their host counterparts at 1e5 subjects, and gpuRos54p is 12 to 16 times faster than Julia’s threaded Rodas5P().
  • Julia’s whole CUDA solve is 3 to 5 times faster: most of rxode2’s time is rxSolve()’s own per-subject setup and output, which every method pays, not the kernel.

Population PK with dosing

bench/gpu-poppk.R simulates 50000 subjects with doses, covariates and dense sampling, so each subject needs one round per record (171 for pk2, 114 for tmdd):

  • pk2: two-compartment PK, oral doses then IV infusions, weight and a time-varying creatinine clearance (non-stiff);
  • tmdd: target-mediated drug disposition with fast binding (stiff).

atol = 1e-8, rtol = 1e-6, times in ms. “CPU build” is gpuBackend = "cpu".

method pk2 tmdd
liblsoda 11506 23910
ros54p 19738 39092
"t54+ros54p" 15418 53742
gpuT54, CPU build 12197 –
gpuRos54p, CPU build 12843 15022
"gpuT54+gpuRos54p", CPU build 12536 18006
gpuT54, OpenCL 11951 –
gpuRos54p, OpenCL 12195 10249
"gpuT54+gpuRos54p", OpenCL 11669 13931
  • On the stiff tmdd, gpuRos54p on the L40 is 2.3 times faster than liblsoda and 3.8 times faster than the host ros54p.
  • On the non-stiff pk2 every method takes about the same time: with a round per record the host event handling, not the integration, sets the time.
  • Explicit methods are not practical for tmdd (t54 took 24 s and gpuT54 on the L40 22 s at 1000 subjects); the AutoSwitch composites detect the stiffness and switch to ros54p, as liblsoda switches to BDF.

How it works

  1. Each subject runs rxode2’s per-subject event loop as a resumable state machine that stops whenever it needs its states integrated from one time to the next.
  2. A round collects every waiting subject and integrates all of them at once: one kernel launch, or the same code compiled for the CPU on cores threads. No R code runs between rounds.
  3. The subjects take their new states, handle their next events, and the loop repeats until all are done.

With options(rxode2.gpuTimeline = TRUE), when no subject’s events depend on its states (observations, boluses and infusions with a fixed rate or duration) a solve takes one launch instead of a round per event interval. Each subject’s events run first without integrating, which records every interval it needs and what its doses add; one launch then integrates each subject’s whole timeline, and the subjects run their events again with the results. The results are the same as the rounds’ (to rounding when several doses into one compartment share a time). On the L40 a SAEM fit took 135 s this way against 112 s with rounds: the device time drops from 58 s to 44 s, but recording and replaying the events adds 37 s of host time.

Statements that depend only on parameters (such as ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)) are computed once per interval rather than at every derivative evaluation (with options(rxode2.optExprExpensive = TRUE) this extends to an exp() or log() of parameters inside a larger expression), and OpenCL work groups are sized so a round of a few thousand subjects spreads over every compute unit (options(rxode2.gpuLocalSize = 0) leaves the size to the driver).

The kernel is generated from the model: its d/dt() (and, for gpuRos54p, the analytic Jacobian) as OpenCL C, the integrator, and the special functions the model calls. It is compiled once per model, method and device and cached for the session.

References

  • Utkarsh, Churavy V, Ma Y, Besard T, Srisuma P, Gymnich T, Gerlach AR, Edelman A, Barbastathis G, Braatz RD, Rackauckas C (2024). Automated translation and accelerated solving of differential equations on multiple GPU platforms. Comput Methods Appl Mech Eng 419:116591.
  • Steinebach G (2023). Construction of Rosenbrock-Wanner method Rodas5P and numerical benchmarks within the Julia Differential Equations package. BIT Numer Math 63:27.
